claim: The Drosophila leg contains 14 muscles which are innervated by just 53 motor neurons.
source: The leg of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, contains 14 muscles which are innervated by just 53 motor neurons (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012; Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020; Soler et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: During forward walking, the fly grips the substrate with the distal segment of its front leg (the tarsus) and flexes the femur-tibia joint, pulling the body forward.
source: During forward walking, the fly grips the substrate with the distal segment of its front leg (the tarsus) and flexes the femur-tibia joint, pulling the body forward (Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Video 4 showing the behavior.

claim: The femur-tibia joint of a walking fly flexes and extends 10–20 times per second, reaching swing speeds of several thousand degrees per second.
source: The femur-tibia joint of a walking fly flexes and extends 10–20 times per second, reaching swing speeds of several thousand degrees per second (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Gowda et al., 2018; Mendes et al., 2013; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Wosnitza et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Three clusters significantly increased their fluorescence when the leg was flexed, referred to as Flexors 1, 2, and 3.
source: Three clusters significantly increased their fluorescence when the leg was flexed (Figure 1C); we refer to these clusters as Flexors 1, 2, and 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: Flexors 2 and 3 were active during most periods of tibia flexion, whereas Flexor 1 was only active during large, fast movements.
source: Flexors 2 and 3 were active during most periods of tibia flexion, whereas Flexor 1 was only active only during large, fast movements (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Flies were able to move the force probe up to 400 μm, reaching speeds of 8 mm/s.
source: Flies were able to move the force probe up to 400 μm, reaching speeds of 8 mm/s (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The fly was capable of producing close to 100 μN of force at the tip of the tibia and changes in force of ~1.3 mN/s.
source: That is, the fly was capable of producing close to 100 μN of force at the tip of the tibia and changes in force of ~1.3 mN/s.
evidence: The claim is derived from measurements of probe displacement and calibrated spring constant.

claim: The mass of the fly is ~1 mg for a weight of ~10 μN.
source: For comparison, the mass of the fly is ~1 mg for a weight of ~10 μN; this means that the femur-tibia joint can produce enough force to lift approximately ten times the fly's body weight.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of fly mass and gravitational force calculation.

claim: The femur-tibia joint can produce enough force to lift approximately ten times the fly's body weight.
source: For comparison, the mass of the fly is ~1 mg for a weight of ~10 μN; this means that the femur-tibia joint can produce enough force to lift approximately ten times the fly's body weight.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the measured force production (~100 μN) compared to the fly's weight (~10 μN).

claim: The highest probe forces and velocities were achieved only when both Flexors 1 and 2 were active together.
source: The highest probe forces and velocities were achieved only when both Flexors 1 and 2 were active together (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: When Flexor 2 was active alone, probe velocities were always lower.
source: When Flexor 2 was active alone, probe velocities were always lower (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The first line (R81A07-Gal4) labels a motor neuron that innervates the high-force motor unit (Flexor 1).
source: The first line (R81A07-Gal4) labels a motor neuron that innervates the high-force motor unit (Figure 2, left) that we identified through calcium imaging (Flexor 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic labeling and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The second line (R22A08-Gal4) labels a neuron that projects to the proximal femur, one of several likely candidates that controls Flexor 2.
source: The second (R22A08-Gal4) labels a neuron that projects to the proximal femur (Figure 2, middle), one of several likely candidates that controls Flexor 2 (Baek and Mann, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 2 and a citation to prior work.

claim: The third line (R35C09-Gal4) labels a single motor neuron that projects to the distal part of the femur.
source: The third line (R35C09-Gal4) labels a single motor neuron that projects to the distal part of the femur, where the signals in our calcium imaging experiments were weak and noisy (Figure 2, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The fast motor neuron is a unique, embryonically born neuron that persists through metamorphosis.
source: Previous studies of motor neuron development suggest that the fast motor neuron is a unique, embryonically born neuron that persists through metamorphosis, whereas the intermediate and slow motor neurons belong to larger cohorts born during metamorphosis (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The intermediate and slow motor neurons belong to larger cohorts born during metamorphosis.
source: Previous studies of motor neuron development suggest that the fast motor neuron is a unique, embryonically born neuron that persists through metamorphosis, whereas the intermediate and slow motor neurons belong to larger cohorts born during metamorphosis (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: 2–5 neurons innervate the proximal muscle fibers in the femur, similar to the intermediate motor neuron.
source: Those studies estimated that 2–5 neurons innervate the proximal muscle fibers in the femur, similar to the intermediate motor neuron, and 8–9 neurons innervate distal muscle fibers, similar to the slow motor neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on estimates from prior developmental studies.

claim: 8–9 neurons innervate distal muscle fibers, similar to the slow motor neuron.
source: Those studies estimated that 2–5 neurons innervate the proximal muscle fibers in the femur, similar to the intermediate motor neuron, and 8–9 neurons innervate distal muscle fibers, similar to the slow motor neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on estimates from prior developmental studies.

claim: The fast motor neuron has an exceptionally large soma (for a Drosophila neuron) and thick dendritic branches.
source: The fast motor neuron has an exceptionally large soma (for a Drosophila neuron) and thick dendritic branches.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: The fast motor neuron's axon has a wide diameter and branches extensively in the femur.
source: Its axon has a wide diameter and branches extensively in the femur (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The intermediate motor neuron has a smaller cell body, thinner dendritic branches, and smaller axonal arborization in the femur.
source: The intermediate motor neuron has a smaller cell body, thinner dendritic branches, and smaller axonal arborization in the femur.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: The slow motor neuron has the smallest cell body, dendrites, and axon of the three.
source: The slow motor neuron has the smallest cell body, dendrites, and axon of the three.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Each motor neuron has a unique dendritic branching pattern within the VNC neuropil.
source: Each motor neuron has a unique dendritic branching pattern within the VNC neuropil.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average resting potential of fast motor neurons was lower (−68 mV) than that of intermediate (−60 mV) and slow (−48 mV) motor neurons.
source: The average resting potential of fast motor neurons was lower (−68 mV) than that of intermediate (−60 mV) and slow (−48 mV) motor neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: While the fast and intermediate neurons were silent at rest, the slow neuron had a resting spike rate of approximately 30 Hz.
source: While the fast and intermediate neurons were silent at rest, the slow neuron had a resting spike rate of approximately 30 Hz (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The input resistance was 150 MΩ for fast motor neurons, 300 MΩ for intermediate motor neurons, and 700 MΩ for slow motor neurons.
source: The input resistance was 150 MΩ for fast motor neurons, 300 MΩ for intermediate motor neurons, and 700 MΩ for slow motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A single fast motor neuron spike produced ~10 μN of force, resulting in a 50 μm movement of the force probe.
source: Aligning probe movement to spike onset showed that a single fast motor neuron spike produced ~10 μN of force, resulting in a 50 μm movement of the force probe (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and force measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: An intermediate neuron spike produced ~1 μN that moved the tibia 5 μm.
source: An intermediate neuron spike produced ~1 μN that moved the tibia 5 μm (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation and force measurement data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: During take-off, the peak force production of the fly leg is ~100 μN.
source: For comparison, during take-off, the peak force production of the fly leg is ~100 μN (Zumstein et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Decreasing slow motor neuron firing produced tibia extension.
source: Decreasing slow motor neuron firing produced tibia extension (Figure 4C,E), suggesting that spontaneous firing in this cell contributes to the resting force on the probe.
evidence: The claim is supported by current injection data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: Bath application of 1 μM MLA led to a decrease in the spontaneous firing rate and reduced the resting force on the probe by ~1.5 μN, or ~15% of the fly's weight.
source: Bath application of 1 μM MLA, an antagonist of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, led to a decrease in the spontaneous firing rate and reduced the resting force on the probe by ~1.5 μN, or ~15% of the fly's weight (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For fast and intermediate neurons, the force produced by two spikes was ~1.6X the force produced by a single spike.
source: For fast and intermediate neurons, the force produced by two spikes was ~1.6X the force produced by a single spike (Figure 4E) and the force-per-spike curves saturated at ~10 spikes (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The force-per-spike curves saturated at ~10 spikes for fast and intermediate neurons.
source: For fast and intermediate neurons, the force produced by two spikes was ~1.6X the force produced by a single spike (Figure 4E) and the force-per-spike curves saturated at ~10 spikes (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The resting spike rate of slow motor neurons maintains constant force on the probe.
source: In contrast, the resting spike rate of slow motor neurons maintains constant force on the probe (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and force measurement data shown in Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: The effect of a spike in the fast and intermediate motor neurons reached half maximal force in ~8.5 ms.
source: For example, the effect of a spike in the fast and intermediate motor neurons reached half maximal force in ~8.5 ms (Figure 4H), whereas the effect of increasing the spike rate in slow motor neurons was gradual and did not reach its peak within 500 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The effect of increasing the spike rate in slow motor neurons was gradual and did not reach its peak within 500 ms.
source: For example, the effect of a spike in the fast and intermediate motor neurons reached half maximal force in ~8.5 ms (Figure 4H), whereas the effect of increasing the spike rate in slow motor neurons was gradual and did not reach its peak within 500 ms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinetic data for slow motor neurons.

claim: The membrane potential of each tibia flexor motor neuron reflected probe movement, even during periods of purely subthreshold activity.
source: The membrane potential of each tibia flexor motor neuron reflected probe movement, even during periods of purely subthreshold activity (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Fast motor neurons typically spiked when the tibia was already flexed and moving.
source: Plots of probe position and movement during example epochs (Figure 5D) illustrate that fast motor neurons typically spiked when the tibia was already flexed and moving.
evidence: The claim is supported by spike-triggered analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The only period during which slow motor neurons were silent was when the tibia was extending (negative probe velocity) or fully extended (zero probe position).
source: In comparison, the only period during which slow motor neurons were silent was when the tibia was extending (negative probe velocity) or fully extended (zero probe position).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spike-triggered analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Neurons lower in the recruitment hierarchy were consistently active when a neuron producing more force was recruited.
source: Neurons lower in the recruitment hierarchy were consistently active when a neuron producing more force was recruited (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recording data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Activity in slow neurons preceded that of intermediate neurons, and activity in intermediate neurons preceded that of fast neurons.
source: In other words, activity in slow neurons preceded that of intermediate neurons, and activity in intermediate neurons preceded that of fast neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the paired recording data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Violations of recruitment order occurred when the fly was rapidly waving its leg, rather than pulling on the force probe.
source: The exceptions occurred when the fly was rapidly waving its leg, rather than pulling on the force probe.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Passive extension of the tibia caused excitatory postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) in all three flexor motor neurons, a response known as a resistance reflex.
source: Passive extension of the tibia caused excitatory postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) in all three flexor motor neurons, a response known as a resistance reflex.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory stimulation data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: PSP amplitude was largest in slow motor neurons and smallest in fast neurons.
source: PSP amplitude was largest in slow motor neurons and smallest in fast neurons (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory stimulation data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Slow motor neurons were exceptionally sensitive to passive tibia movement: a 1° change in tibia angle resulted in a significant change in firing rate.
source: Slow motor neurons were exceptionally sensitive to passive tibia movement: a 1° change in tibia angle resulted in a significant change in firing rate (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory stimulation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Extremely fast extension movements were sufficient to evoke single spikes in intermediate neurons.
source: Extremely fast extension movements were sufficient to evoke single spikes in intermediate neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but we never observed feedback-evoked spikes in fast motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory stimulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: We never observed feedback-evoked spikes in fast motor neurons.
source: Extremely fast extension movements were sufficient to evoke single spikes in intermediate neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but we never observed feedback-evoked spikes in fast motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of observed spikes in fast motor neurons during sensory stimulation experiments.

claim: The Drosophila FeCO is comprised of ~150 mechanosensory neurons that encode position, movement, and vibration of the femur-tibia joint.
source: The Drosophila FeCO is comprised of ~150 mechanosensory neurons that encode position, movement, and vibration of the femur-tibia joint (Mamiya et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Stimulating FeCO neurons caused the fly to extend and then flex its tibia in a rapid and stereotyped manner.
source: Stimulating FeCO neurons caused the fly to extend and then flex its tibia in a rapid and stereotyped manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Motor neuron responses to FeCO stimulation increased from slow motor neurons to fast motor neurons.
source: Motor neuron responses to FeCO stimulation increased from slow motor neurons to fast motor neurons, consistent with responses to passive stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chrimson expression in FeCO neurons reduced motor neuron responses to passive leg movements compared to control flies.
source: In interpreting these experiments, it is important to note that Chrimson expression in FeCO neurons reduced motor neuron responses to passive leg movements compared to control flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of fast motor neurons caused rapid flexion of the tibia.
source: Activation of fast motor neurons caused rapid flexion of the tibia (Figure 7B,C, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 7B-C and Video 3.

claim: Activation of intermediate neurons caused slower tibia flexion, while activation of slow neurons caused even slower contractions, often followed by unexpected, prolonged tibia extension.
source: Activation of intermediate neurons caused slower tibia flexion, while activation of slow neurons caused even slower contractions, often followed by unexpected, prolonged tibia extension.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic manipulation data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Silencing each motor neuron type did not consistently evoke leg movements, though silencing the full motor neuron population resulted in paralysis.
source: Silencing each motor neuron type did not consistently evoke leg movements, though silencing the full motor neuron population resulted in paralysis (Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic silencing data shown in Video 4.

claim: Activation of the fast motor neuron caused the tibia of the front leg to persistently flex, thus, interrupting walking.
source: Activation of the fast motor neuron caused the tibia of the front leg to persistently flex, thus, interrupting walking (Figure 7E, Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E and Video 5.

claim: Activation of the slow motor neurons interrupted walking because the fly reacted by extending its tibia.
source: Activation of the slow motor neurons also interrupted walking (Figure 7E), but this was because the fly reacted by extending its tibia, as when the legs were unloaded (Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E and Video 7.

claim: Activation of the intermediate motor neuron appeared to cause the flies to transiently increase their walking speed.
source: Unlike the other two cells, activation of the intermediate motor neuron appeared to cause the flies to transiently increase their walking speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: Activation of the intermediate motor neuron in stationary flies caused them to start walking.
source: Activation of the intermediate motor neuron in stationary flies also caused them to start walking (Figure 7E–F, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7E-F and Video 6.

claim: Silencing of fast and intermediate neurons decreased the probability that a stationary fly would initiate walking compared to controls.
source: However, silencing of fast and intermediate neurons decreased the probability that a stationary fly would initiate walking compared to controls (Figure 7H, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7H and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: Leg motor neurons are recruited in a specific order: small, low gain motor neurons that generate weak forces are recruited first, and larger, more powerful motor neurons are recruited later.
source: We found that leg motor neurons are recruited in a specific order: small, low gain motor neurons that generate weak forces are recruited first, and larger, more powerful motor neurons are recruited later (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by recruitment order data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback has the greatest effect on the slow motor neuron: tibia movements of less than 1° significantly impact slow motor neuron firing.
source: Consistent with this recruitment order, proprioceptive feedback has the greatest effect on the slow motor neuron: tibia movements of less than 1° significantly impact slow motor neuron firing (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory feedback data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback has a much smaller effect on the firing rate of intermediate and fast motor neurons.
source: By comparison, proprioceptive feedback has a much smaller effect on the firing rate of intermediate and fast motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of sensory feedback data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Flies fail to initiate walking if unable to recruit slow motor neurons at the bottom of the recruitment hierarchy.
source: For example, flies fail to initiate walking if unable to recruit slow motor neurons at the bottom of the recruitment hierarchy.
evidence: The claim is inferred from optogenetic silencing data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A human leg is innervated by over 150,000 motor neurons and a single calf muscle is innervated by over 600 motor neurons.
source: For example, a human leg is innervated by over 150,000 motor neurons and a single calf muscle is innervated by over 600 motor neurons (Kernell, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The size principle states that small motor neurons, with lower spike thresholds, are recruited prior to larger neurons, which have higher spike thresholds.
source: Subsequent work identified mechanisms associated with the recruitment order and synthesized these findings as the size principle, which states that small motor neurons, with lower spike thresholds, are recruited prior to larger neurons, which have higher spike thresholds (Henneman et al., 1965a; Henneman et al., 1965b; Henneman and Olson, 1965; Mcphedran et al., 1965; Mendell, 2005; McPhedran et al., 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Evidence for the size principle has been provided by electrophysiological analysis of motor neurons in a number of species, from crayfish to humans.
source: Evidence for the size principle has been provided by electrophysiological analysis of motor neurons in a number of species, from crayfish to humans (Gabriel et al., 2003; Hill and Cattaert, 2008; McLean and Dougherty, 2015; Milner-Brown et al., 1973; Sasaki and Burrows, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: A simplifying assumption of the size principle is that all motor neurons within a pool receive identical presynaptic input, such that recruitment order is entirely dictated by the gradient of motor neuron excitability.
source: A simplifying assumption of the size principle is that all motor neurons within a pool receive identical presynaptic input, such that recruitment order is entirely dictated by the gradient of motor neuron excitability.
evidence: The claim is based on established understanding of the size principle.

claim: Recordings in vertebrates have found that presynaptic inputs may vary within a motor pool.
source: However, recordings in vertebrates have found that presynaptic inputs may vary within a motor pool (McLean and Dougherty, 2015) and that recruitment order can change during specific movements (Desnedt and Gidaux, 1981; Kishore et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Smith et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Recruitment order can change during specific movements.
source: However, recordings in vertebrates have found that presynaptic inputs may vary within a motor pool (McLean and Dougherty, 2015) and that recruitment order can change during specific movements (Desnedt and Gidaux, 1981; Kishore et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Smith et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Tibia motor neurons receive distinct proprioceptive feedback signals.
source: However, we also find that fast, intermediate, and slow motor neurons receive distinct proprioceptive feedback signals, suggesting that the size principle is not the only mechanism that dictates motor neuron recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory feedback data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The size principle is not the only mechanism that dictates motor neuron recruitment.
source: However, we also find that fast, intermediate, and slow motor neurons receive distinct proprioceptive feedback signals, suggesting that the size principle is not the only mechanism that dictates motor neuron recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of distinct proprioceptive feedback signals.

claim: In addition to the size principle, heterogeneous input from premotor circuits is likely to play an important role in coordinating neural activity within a motor pool.
source: Thus, in addition to the size principle, heterogeneous input from premotor circuits is likely to play an important role in coordinating neural activity within a motor pool.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed violations of the size principle and distinct feedback signals.

claim: Tibia flexor motor neurons generally follow a recruitment order in accordance with the size principle.
source: Although tibia motor neurons generally follow a recruitment order in accordance with the size principle (Figure 5), we found that the dynamics of proprioceptive feedback vary across motor neurons within the pool (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by recruitment order data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The dynamics of proprioceptive feedback vary across motor neurons within the pool.
source: Although tibia motor neurons generally follow a recruitment order in accordance with the size principle (Figure 5), we found that the dynamics of proprioceptive feedback vary across motor neurons within the pool (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by sensory feedback data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A small but significant proportion of behavioral events violated recruitment order.
source: We also observed a small but significant proportion of behavioral events in which recruitment order was violated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tibia flexor motor neuron pool may share some presynaptic inputs, but they are not identical.
source: These data suggest that although the tibia flexor motor neuron pool may share some presynaptic inputs, they are not identical.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of distinct feedback signals and recruitment order violations.

claim: Motor control of the fly tibia is more complex than a straightforward implementation of the size principle.
source: Thus, motor control of the fly tibia is more complex than a straightforward implementation of the size principle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed complexity of feedback signals and recruitment patterns.

claim: The effect of proprioceptive feedback varies across a pool of motor neurons controlling the cat leg.
source: For instance, the effect of proprioceptive feedback varies across a pool of motor neurons controlling the cat leg (Heckman and Binder, 1988; Heckman and Binder, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: During rapid escape behaviors in zebrafish, slow motor neurons can completely drop out of the population firing pattern.
source: During rapid escape behaviors in zebrafish, slow motor neurons can completely drop out of the population firing pattern (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Muscles controlling human fingers can change recruitment order based on movement direction.
source: Muscles controlling human fingers can change recruitment order based on movement direction (Desmedt and Godaux, 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Motor neurons receive coincident excitation and inhibition, which could underlie selective de-recruitment.
source: For example, recordings in turtles and zebrafish have shown that motor neurons receive coincident excitation and inhibition, which could underlie selective de-recruitment (Berg et al., 2007; Kishore et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Zebrafish spinal cord premotor neurons provide patterned inhibition to speed-specific circuits.
source: Zebrafish spinal cord premotor neurons provide patterned inhibition to speed-specific circuits (Callahan et al., 2019; Menelaou et al., 2019) and can flexibly switch between different motor neuron recruitment patterns (Bagnall and McLean, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Zebrafish spinal cord premotor neurons can flexibly switch between different motor neuron recruitment patterns.
source: Zebrafish spinal cord premotor neurons provide patterned inhibition to speed-specific circuits (Callahan et al., 2019; Menelaou et al., 2019) and can flexibly switch between different motor neuron recruitment patterns (Bagnall and McLean, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: The muscles that control flexion of the Drosophila tibia are innervated by approximately 15 motor neurons.
source: The muscles that control flexion of the Drosophila tibia are innervated by approximately 15 motor neurons (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The fast tibia flexor motor neuron labeled by R81A07-Gal4 is the only motor neuron that innervates the large tibia flexor muscle fibers in the middle of the femur.
source: The fast tibia flexor motor neuron labeled by R81A07-Gal4 is the only motor neuron that innervates the large tibia flexor muscle fibers in the middle of the femur (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fast motor neuron has the largest axon of any motor neuron in the femur.
source: Because it has the largest axon of any motor neuron in the femur, the fast motor neuron also produces the largest extracellular spikes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical and electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The slow tibia flexor motor neuron labeled by R35C09-Gal4 is one of 8–9 motor neurons that innervates tibia flexor muscle fibers located at the distal tip of the femur.
source: The slow tibia flexor motor neuron labeled by R35C09-Gal4 is one of 8–9 motor neurons that innervates tibia flexor muscle fibers located at the distal tip of the femur.
evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies and genetic labeling.

claim: The R35C09-Gal4 neuron is among the weakest within the group of distal flexor motor neurons.
source: Measurements of force production from other motor neurons that innervated this distal region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) suggest that the R35C09-Gal4 neuron is among the weakest within this group.
evidence: The claim is inferred from force production measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 2–5 neurons innervate nearby muscle fibers in the proximal region of the femur.
source: Previous anatomical studies suggest that 2–5 neurons innervate nearby muscle fibers in the proximal region of the femur.
evidence: The claim is based on prior anatomical studies.

claim: The gradient of properties applies to other neurons in the tibia flexor motor pool.
source: Our recordings of other tibia flexor motor neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) were consistent with the gradient of properties we describe in detail for three identified motor neurons, which suggests that the relationship between anatomy, physiology, and force production applies to other neurons in the tibia flexor motor pool.
evidence: The claim is inferred from recordings of additional motor neurons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the metathoracic leg of the locust, a single tibia flexor muscle is innervated by nine motor neurons that were classified into three groups: fast, intermediate, and slow.
source: In the metathoracic leg of the locust, a single tibia flexor muscle is innervated by nine motor neurons that were also classified into three groups: fast, intermediate, and slow (Burrows and Hoyle, 1973; Phillips, 1981; Sasaki and Burrows, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Different motor neurons within the locust tibia flexor pool lie along a gradient of intrinsic properties.
source: Different motor neurons within this pool lie along a gradient of intrinsic properties (Sasaki and Burrows, 1998) and are sensitive to different types of proprioceptive feedback, such as position vs. velocity or fast vs. slow movements (Field and Burrows, 1982; Newland and Kondoh, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Locust tibia flexor motor neurons are sensitive to different types of proprioceptive feedback, such as position vs. velocity or fast vs. slow movements.
source: Different motor neurons within this pool lie along a gradient of intrinsic properties (Sasaki and Burrows, 1998) and are sensitive to different types of proprioceptive feedback, such as position vs. velocity or fast vs. slow movements (Field and Burrows, 1982; Newland and Kondoh, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The femur of the stick insect is innervated by flexor motor neurons that were described as slow, semi-fast, and fast, based on their intrinsic properties and firing patterns during behavior.
source: The femur of the stick insect is innervated by flexor motor neurons that were also described as slow, semi-fast, and fast, based on their intrinsic properties and firing patterns during behavior (Bässler, 1993; Schmidt et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Most arthropods possess GABAergic motor neurons that directly inhibit leg muscles.
source: Flies differ from these other invertebrates in one major respect: while most arthropods possess GABAergic motor neurons that directly inhibit leg muscles, holometabolous insects such as Drosophila do not (Schmid et al., 1999; Witten and Truman, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Holometabolous insects such as Drosophila do not possess GABAergic motor neurons that directly inhibit leg muscles.
source: Flies differ from these other invertebrates in one major respect: while most arthropods possess GABAergic motor neurons that directly inhibit leg muscles, holometabolous insects such as Drosophila do not (Schmid et al., 1999; Witten and Truman, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A transgenic line for GABAergic neurons (Gad1-Gal4) does not label any axons in the Drosophila leg.
source: Indeed, we found that a transgenic line for GABAergic neurons (Gad1-Gal4; Diao et al., 2015) does not label any axons in the Drosophila leg (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: The presence of inhibitory motor neurons has been proposed as a key underlying reason why insects have been able to achieve flexible motor control with small numbers of motor neurons.
source: The presence of inhibitory motor neurons has been proposed as a key underlying reason why insects have been able to achieve flexible motor control with small numbers of motor neurons (Belanger, 2005; Wolf, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Fly legs are innervated by neurons that release neuromodulators, such as octopamine, which could underlie flexible tuning of muscle excitability.
source: Fly legs are innervated by neurons that release neuromodulators, such as octopamine, which could underlie flexible tuning of muscle excitability (Zumstein et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work and is speculative about the functional role.

claim: Activity in slow motor neurons produces small, low force movements, while fast motor neuron activity produces fast, high amplitude movements.
source: Activity in slow motor neurons produces small, low force movements, while fast motor neuron activity produces fast, high amplitude movements.
evidence: The claim is inferred from force production data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback may continuously modulate the firing rate of slow motor neurons for precise stabilization of posture during standing or grooming.
source: Thus, proprioceptive feedback may continuously modulate the firing rate of slow motor neurons for precise stabilization of posture during standing or grooming.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed strong proprioceptive feedback to slow motor neurons.

claim: Rapid, stereotyped movements like escape are likely to use fast motor neurons whose activity is less dependent on sensory feedback.
source: In contrast to the postural movements controlled by slow motor neurons, rapid, stereotyped movements like escape (Card and Dickinson, 2008; Zumstein et al., 2004) are likely to use fast motor neurons whose activity is less dependent on sensory feedback.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed weak proprioceptive feedback to fast motor neurons and citations to prior work on escape behaviors.

claim: Slow contracting muscle fibers use aerobic metabolism and take advantage of energy stores in the form of glycogen, while fast muscle fibers are anaerobic and lack energy stores, leading to more rapid fatigue.
source: This division of labor may also provide energy efficiency: slow contracting muscle fibers use aerobic metabolism and take advantage of energy stores in the form of glycogen, while fast muscle fibers are anaerobic and lack energy stores, leading to more rapid fatigue (Kernell, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Stick insects walking on treadmills typically recruit fast motor neurons only during fast walking and, in that case, late in the stance phase.
source: In a similar manner, stick insects walking on treadmills typically recruit fast motor neurons only during fast walking and, in that case, late in the stance phase.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from prior studies of stick insect locomotion.

claim: As friction on the treadmill increases, fast neurons are recruited earlier during stance in stick insects.
source: But as friction on the treadmill increases, fast neurons are recruited earlier during stance (Gabriel et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Leg kinematics and force production change as insects walk up or down inclines.
source: Leg kinematics and force production also change as insects walk up or down inclines (Dallmann et al., 2019; Wöhrl et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: When locusts and cockroaches are forced to walk upside-down, fast flexor neurons are recruited to allow the animal to grip the substrate.
source: When locusts (Duch and Pflüger, 1995) and cockroaches (Larsen et al., 1995; Watson and Ritzmann, 1997) are forced to walk upside-down, fast flexor neurons are recruited to allow the animal to grip the substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Small changes in body posture can have a large effect on which motor neurons are recruited during target reaching movements in locusts.
source: This context-dependence is not limited to walking: small changes in body posture can have a large effect on which motor neurons are recruited during target reaching movements in locusts (Page et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: Tibia flexor motor neurons outnumber the extensor neurons.
source: Tibia flexor motor neurons outnumber the extensor neurons (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012), and thus are likely to possess a shallower gradient of intrinsic and functional properties, as has been found in crayfish (Hill and Cattaert, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Tibia flexor motor neurons are likely to possess a shallower gradient of intrinsic and functional properties than extensor neurons, as has been found in crayfish.
source: Tibia flexor motor neurons outnumber the extensor neurons (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012), and thus are likely to possess a shallower gradient of intrinsic and functional properties, as has been found in crayfish (Hill and Cattaert, 2008).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the number of motor neurons and a citation to prior work in crayfish.

claim: Invertebrate muscles exhibit polyneural innervation, such that a given muscle fiber may be innervated by multiple motor neurons.
source: Invertebrate muscles also exhibit polyneural innervation, such that a given muscle fiber may be innervated by multiple motor neurons (Brierley et al., 2012; Hoyle, 1983; Sasaki and Burrows, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Polyneural innervation could allow independent activation of motor neurons in order to use the same muscle fibers during different contexts.
source: Polyneural innervation could allow independent activation of motor neurons in order to use the same muscle fibers during different contexts, or it could make the force produced by one motor neuron dependent on coincident activity in another motor neuron (Sasaki and Burrows, 1998).
evidence: The claim is speculative about the functional implications of polyneural innervation, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Polyneural innervation could make the force produced by one motor neuron dependent on coincident activity in another motor neuron.
source: Polyneural innervation could allow independent activation of motor neurons in order to use the same muscle fibers during different contexts, or it could make the force produced by one motor neuron dependent on coincident activity in another motor neuron (Sasaki and Burrows, 1998).
evidence: The claim is speculative about the functional implications of polyneural innervation, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Studies of motor control in the fly VNC are now possible thanks to an increasing catalog of genetically-identified cell types.
source: Studies of motor control in the fly VNC are now possible thanks to an increasing catalog of genetically-identified cell types (Lacin et al., 2019; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019), connectomic reconstruction with serial-section EM (Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020) and the ability to image from VNC neurons in walking flies (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent published work.

claim: Connectomic reconstruction with serial-section EM enables studies of motor control in the fly VNC.
source: Studies of motor control in the fly VNC are now possible thanks to an increasing catalog of genetically-identified cell types (Lacin et al., 2019; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019), connectomic reconstruction with serial-section EM (Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020) and the ability to image from VNC neurons in walking flies (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent published work.

claim: The ability to image from VNC neurons in walking flies enables studies of motor control in the fly VNC.
source: Studies of motor control in the fly VNC are now possible thanks to an increasing catalog of genetically-identified cell types (Lacin et al., 2019; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019), connectomic reconstruction with serial-section EM (Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020) and the ability to image from VNC neurons in walking flies (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent published work.

claim: The leg motor neurons described provide valuable targets for understanding the coordinated development of motor neuron and muscle properties.
source: The leg motor neurons we describe also provide valuable targets for understanding the coordinated development of motor neuron and muscle properties (Enriquez et al., 2015; Venkatasubramanian et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative about future applications, with citations to prior work on development.

claim: Drosophila will be a useful complement to other model organisms in understanding the neural basis of flexible motor control.
source: We anticipate that Drosophila will be a useful complement to other model organisms in understanding the neural basis of flexible motor control.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the future utility of Drosophila as a model system.

claim: The force probe had a spring constant of k = 0.2234 µN/µm.
source: We measured the spring constant by positioning the force probe over an analytical balance. A glass coverslip was oriented vertically on edge in a piece of wax on the balance, and the tip of the force probe was positioned at the top edge of the coverslip. We then moved the micromanipulator to different positions. The 'mass' of the force probe was multiplied by gravity to give the force at that position. We then fit a linear relationship between force and position to measure the spring constant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). The force probe we used for experiments in this study had a spring constant of k = 0.2234 µN/µm and protruded approximately 1.5 cm past the end of the micropipette.
evidence: The claim is supported by calibration measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The force probe had an effective mass of m = 0.1702 mg and drag coefficient of c = 0.1377 kg/s.
source: To measure these properties, we 'flicked' the force probe by moving it to different positions with a glass micropipette, abruptly letting go, and allowing the probe to relax back to rest (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). We imaged the position of the probe at 1.2 kHz with a restricted region of interest, and extracted dynamical parameters m = 0.1702 mg and c = 0.1377 kg/s.
evidence: The claim is supported by dynamical measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The probe was slightly under-damped with a relaxation time constant of 2.5 ms and oscillation period of 5.8 ms.
source: The probe was slightly under-damped with a relaxation time constant of 2.5 ms and oscillation period of 5.8 ms, such that when imaging spontaneous movements at 170 Hz, the probe would effectively come to rest within one frame.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the measured dynamical parameters.

claim: The liquid junction potential for the whole cell recordings was −13 mV.
source: The liquid junction potential for the whole cell recordings was −13 mV (Gouwens and Wilson, 2009). We corrected the membrane voltages reported in the paper by post hoc subtraction of the junction potential.
evidence: The claim is based on a calculation method cited from prior work.

claim: Caffeine application did not increase activity on the leg electrodes during periods of rest.
source: Caffeine's effects have been reported to be due to dopamine receptor agonism (Nall et al., 2016). Caffeine application did not increase activity on the leg electrodes during periods of rest.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during experiments with caffeine application.

claim: Slow motor neuron spike detection was difficult during large current injections because spikes became very small.
source: However, two cases typically caused spikes to become very difficult to unambiguously identify in slow motor neurons. First, during large current injections and the resulting depolarization, the spikes became very small and difficult to identify (Figure 4). High frequency spikes were clear in the raw voltage, and the leg moved, so we do not believe the neurons entered depolarization block.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during current injection experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Prolonged self-generated flexion could depolarize slow motor neurons to the point that spike detection was difficult, possibly because of large synaptic conductances that decreased input resistance.
source: Second, prolonged self-generated flexion could also depolarize slow motor neurons to the point that spike detection was difficult, we speculate because of large synaptic conductances that decreased input resistance.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations during spontaneous movements.

claim: Spike detection worked perfectly during high spike rates evoked by sensory feedback in slow motor neurons.
source: By contrast, spike detection worked perfectly during high spike rates evoked by sensory feedback (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on observations during sensory stimulation experiments shown in Figure 6.
